Title: Training for the work you do
Our paraphrase: Every worker is trained in the safe practices and emergency procedures for their own job, such as pole-top and manhole rescue. The more risk a task carries, the more thorough the training, and a worker must show proficiency before the training counts as complete.

Title: What makes a worker qualified
Our paraphrase: A qualified worker can tell live parts from other parts and can find the voltage of exposed live parts. They also know the safe distances for the voltages they face, how to use protective gear and insulated tools, and how to spot and control electrical hazards.

Title: Know the line before you start
Our paraphrase: Before work near a line or equipment, find out its voltage, whether hazardous induced voltage is present, where grounds and other circuits are, and the condition of poles and the weather. This information feeds the plan for the job.

Title: Job briefing
Our paraphrase: Before each job the person in charge briefs the crew on the hazards, the work steps, special precautions, how energy sources are controlled, and the protective equipment needed. Repetitive work needs a briefing at the start of each day or shift, and another one whenever conditions change in a way that affects safety.

Title: Test the air before entering an enclosed space
Our paraphrase: Before anyone enters an enclosed space, the air is tested for too little oxygen first and then for flammable gas, using a direct-reading meter. If either problem is found, forced-air ventilation is used or, when flammable gas is only at safe levels, continuous monitoring. When continuous forced-air ventilation is the method, it starts before entry and runs until everyone has left.

Title: Attendant at the opening
Our paraphrase: While people work in an enclosed space, a first-aid-trained attendant stays right outside to help where traffic near the opening could cause trouble. The attendant may do other chores as long as they keep watching the people inside and the entry area.

Title: Treat lines as live unless cleared
Our paraphrase: Only qualified workers may work on or with exposed live lines or equipment, and only qualified workers may work in areas with unguarded, uninsulated live parts of 50 volts or more. Any line or equipment counts as energized unless it was made dead under the lockout rules for generation or the clearance procedure for lines.

Title: Two-person rule
Our paraphrase: At least two workers must be present to install, remove or repair lines energized above 600 volts, to work on dead lines or equipment such as transformers where a worker could touch parts energized above 600 volts, to use mechanical equipment near such parts, and for other work that is just as hazardous. The rule does not apply to routine switching where site conditions allow it safely, to work with live-line tools from out of reach of live parts, or to emergency repairs that protect the public.

Title: Safe approach distance and insulation
Our paraphrase: The employer sets a minimum approach distance based on voltage, and nobody, and no conductive object they carry, goes closer than that. The exceptions are when the worker is insulated from the live part, the live part is insulated from the worker, or live-line barehand methods are used.

Title: Arc flash protection
Our paraphrase: The employer finds out which workers face flames or electric arcs and estimates the heat energy they could be exposed to. Clothing must not melt onto the skin or keep burning. When the estimate is above 2.0 calories per square centimeter, workers wear clothing and gear with an arc rating at least equal to the estimate, covering the whole body except where limited exceptions for hands, feet, face and head apply.

Title: Clearance and tagging to make a line dead
Our paraphrase: Where a system operator controls the line, the crew member in charge of the clearance asks the operator to make the section dead. Every switch and other source is opened, made inoperable where the design allows, and tagged, including remote and automatic controls. Once the operator grants clearance, the line is tested with a voltage detector and protective grounds are installed, and only then does it count as deenergized; where no operator is in charge, or one crew works with a visible disconnect under its sole control, some steps change.

Title: Restoring power safely
Our paraphrase: Nobody starts to reenergize a line at a disconnect until all protective grounds are removed, every crew has released its clearance, all workers are clear, and the tags at that disconnect are removed. Only the worker in charge who requested the clearance may release it, unless responsibility was formally transferred, and tags stay on until that release.

Title: Ground a dead line before working it
Our paraphrase: To work a line as dead, it must first be deenergized under the clearance procedure and then grounded so workers cannot face a dangerous voltage difference. Skipping grounds is allowed only if installing them is impractical or more dangerous, and then there must be no chance of contact with another live source and no induced voltage.

Title: Test, then ground, in the right order
Our paraphrase: Before any ground is installed, the line is tested to confirm there is no voltage, unless a ground is already in place. When attaching a ground, connect the ground end first and then the line end using a live-line tool, and when removing, take off the line end first and the ground end last. For lines at 600 volts or less, other insulating equipment can be allowed under conditions.

Title: Fall protection on poles and lifts
Our paraphrase: Workers in an aerial lift use a travel restraint or fall arrest system. Anyone on a pole, tower or similar structure more than 4 feet above the ground uses fall arrest, work-positioning or fall restraint equipment unless other qualifying fall protection is provided. Qualified climbers must also use it while climbing or changing position unless that is infeasible or creates a greater hazard, but trainees and other unqualified workers must use it any time they are above 4 feet.

Title: Cranes and trucks near live lines
Our paraphrase: Equipment must keep the safe approach distance from live lines, and a second worker watches the distance and warns the operator unless the operator can judge it alone. If the equipment could become energized, the lines are covered, the equipment is insulated and kept back, or the crew uses grounding, bonding, ground mats and barriers.

Title: Check the pole before climbing or setting
Our paraphrase: Make sure a pole can take the extra or uneven load of climbing and new equipment, and brace it if not. When a pole is set or moved near a live conductor it must not touch it, workers use protective equipment or insulated tools, and open pole holes are guarded or watched.

Title: Induced voltage on new lines
Our paraphrase: A line strung beside a live one can pick up dangerous voltage from it. The employer estimates the induced voltage or assumes it is hazardous, and places temporary grounds so workers are not exposed to harmful voltage differences.

Title: Getting in and out of manholes and vaults
Our paraphrase: Use a ladder or other climbing device to enter or leave a manhole or underground vault deeper than 4 feet, and never climb by stepping on cables or hangers. Before anyone lowers tools or material into the opening, each person working below must be clear of the area directly under it.

Title: Attendant and radios at energized vaults
Our paraphrase: When work goes on in a manhole or vault with live equipment, a first-aid-trained person waits on the surface right by the entrance. Everyone on the job keeps reliable two-way contact, such as radios.

Title: Guarding the work area
Our paraphrase: Before working near road or foot traffic, crews put out warning signs, flags and traffic-control devices to warn and steer people. Barricades protect where more protection is needed, open excavations are barricaded, and warning lights are displayed at night.

Title: Backfeed from generators and the secondary side
Our paraphrase: A line that looks dead can be fed back from customer generation or from the secondary side of a transformer. If the line may be backfed, treat it as live under the live-work rules, or make it dead and ground it under the clearance and grounding rules.
